captions.s02-vec2d: Two numbers are a point, and the arrow from the origin to it. The array [3, 2] and the arrow are the same thing.
captions.s03-vec3d: Three numbers are a point in 3D: three along x, two up along y, one toward you along z, and the view turns so the depth reads. Real models just keep adding numbers.

captions.s05-matmul-example: Multiplying a vector by a matrix gives a new vector. This operation is called a linear transformation. For this matrix the arrow shears sideways: [1, 1] becomes [1.5, 1].
captions.s06-matmul-variants: Different matrices move the same vector in different ways. It cycles through the identity, two shears and a stretch. Training is what finds the useful ones.

captions.s07-dot-intro: The dot product multiplies matching entries and adds them up. Pointing the same way gives a big positive number, at right angles zero, and opposite ways a negative one.

captions.s09-ideas-axes: If each dimension is an idea, a vector is a mix of ideas. Sand is desert and non-living; rock is almost purely non-living. (A toy: real dimensions are never this readable.)
captions.s10-ideas-dot: Sand and rock are both non-living, so their dot product is positive. Sand and fern point opposite ways, so theirs is negative.
captions.s11-sandstone: Multiply sand by the right matrix and it shears toward rock, landing on sandstone. Transforming vectors like this is all a transformer layer does.

captions.s12-box-words: Give a transformer a sentence and it predicts the next word.
captions.s13-loop-words: That is the loop: predict one word, append it, feed everything back in, and stop when what comes out looks like an end.

captions.s14-not-words: Models read tokens, not words. Qwen3.8-27B's real tokenizer turns these 5 words into 8 tokens. The dot marks a leading space, which is part of the token.

captions.s15-model-folder: The real Qwen3.8-27B folder: a vocabulary (tokenizer.json), a config, and 55.6 GB of numbers in 18 safetensors shards. To follow along you only need the first two.

captions.s16-vocab-file: The vocabulary is a numbered list: 248,044 tokens plus 33 special ones. Punctuation and letters come first, then words and word pieces from many languages. (Real entries from the file.)
captions.s17-tokenizer: Each piece is looked up in the vocabulary and replaced by its number. From here on, the model only ever sees numbers. (Real Qwen3.8-27B ids.)

captions.s18-unknown-word: A word that is not in the vocabulary is split into pieces that are, so rare words just cost more tokens. (Real ids. The Arabic word reads right to left, so its first piece is on the right.)

captions.s19-embedding-table: A token's number is a row index into one huge table: 248,320 rows of 5,120 numbers, 1.27 billion in all. Row 628 is " can", and these are its real first 8 values. (The grid is a stylised sample.)
captions.s21-hidden-size: The length of every row is the model's hidden_size, read straight from config.json. Bigger models choose longer vectors.

captions.s20-row-is-vector: Each number says how much of one idea the token carries. On the left, the real first 64 numbers of " can"; on the right, the toy camel: 0.75 desert plus 0.55 living.

captions.s22-random-start: Before training, the embedding table is noise: random numbers pointing in random directions. Nothing about cats or dogs is in there yet.
captions.s23-training-pair: Take a sentence from the training data, feed in the first part, and compare the guess with the real next word. (The guess "dog" is made up; an untrained model guesses badly.)
captions.s24-error: The error is how far the guess was from the answer, and it decides how much to change. (Toy probabilities. Real training measures the error as cross-entropy, the log of the probability given to the right word, but the idea is the same.)

captions.s25-derivative: The slope of the error says which way to nudge a number, and by how much: steep means a big nudge, flat means we are close. (A toy error curve over one number w, with a step size of 0.3.)
captions.s26-nudge-all: After millions of tiny corrections the numbers stop being random, and similar tokens end up pointing similar ways. That is where embeddings come from. (Toy positions in 2 dimensions.)

captions.s27-four-stages: Inside the box are four stages: the embedder we just met, attention and feed-forward doing the thinking, and sampling picking the word.
captions.s28-layers-repeat: Attention and feed-forward repeat as one block, 64 times in Qwen3.8-27B. (Most of its attention layers are a linear-attention variant; the idea is the same.)

captions.s29-ball-sentence: The real Qwen3.8-27B tokenizer on "I'm tarballing the oddball photos of golf balls". Both "ball" pieces are token 3826, so the model starts them from the very same vector.
captions.s30-ball-3d: Golf ball, oddball and tarball are the same starting vector pushed in three different directions. Working out which push applies is attention's job. (A toy in 3 numbers; the real vector has 5,120.)
captions.s31-influence: Each token is shaped by the tokens around it: thick arcs are strong influence, faint ones almost none. (The arc sizes come from the toy numbers in the next figures.)

captions.s32-qkv-matrices: Three more tables of numbers, Wq, Wk and Wv, start random and are tuned in training like everything else. Applied to the same embedding, they give a query, a key and a value. (Real Qwen3.8-27B shapes, where Wq's 12,288 outputs include a gate as well as the queries. The cells are a toy picture.)
captions.s33-query: The query is the embedding times Wq: what this token is looking for. The first ball is looking for a word that modifies it. (Toy numbers in 2 dimensions.)

captions.s34-key: The key is the embedding times Wk: what kind of influence this token has to offer. Tar's key says: I am a modifier.
captions.s35-value: The value is the embedding times Wv: what gets blended into another token when that token's query matches this key. Tar's value would make the ball tar-like.

captions.s36-score-table: Every cell is one dot product: how well this token's query lines up with that token's key. The first ball lines up with tar, the second with odd, and balls with golf. (Toy numbers; real models also weigh how far apart the tokens are.)
captions.s37-softmax-weights: Softmax turns the first ball's scores into weights: raise e to each score, then divide by the total, so they are all positive and add up to 1.

captions.s38-apply-values: The weights decide how much of each value to add: tar's counts most, golf's barely. Sum them, add the sum to the ball's embedding, and the vector is sheared toward tarball. (In this toy the ball's own value is zero.)
captions.s39-attention-result: Both balls started as the very same vector. Context turned one into a tarball and the other into an oddball, and moved balls toward golf.

captions.s40-world-cup: Some answers are not in the sentence. Nothing in "Who won the 2026 FIFA World Cup?" says Spain, so something has to move this vector toward it. (Real tokenization; a toy vector on two readable axes.)

captions.s41-wu-wd-intro: Wu widens 5,120 numbers to 17,408, and Wd brings them back. In between, something happens to the long vector: the next figures open each piece.

captions.s42-wu-detectors: Each column of Wu is a question about the token, scored with a dot product. Training text in which Spain won the 2026 World Cup left one column that fires on exactly this question. (Toy questions; the real ones are not human-readable.)
captions.s43-silence: Weak matches are switched off and strong ones pass through, so the capital-city and food detectors go silent. (A toy hard cut at 0.5; real models use a smooth activation.)
captions.s44-wd-shear: Each surviving detector scales its row of Wd, and their sum is added to the token, shearing it toward Spain. (Toy numbers.)

captions.s45-ffn-flow: The feed-forward step: Wu asks 17,408 questions at once, the weak answers are silenced, and Wd turns the strong ones into a change that is added back onto the token. (Real shapes. Qwen3.8-27B also has a gate_proj and a smooth SiLU, folded here into one silencing step.)

captions.s45-ffn-recap: Attention is the only place tokens talk to each other: context from this sentence. Feed-forward works on one token at a time, with knowledge stored during training.

captions.s46-one-layer: One layer is attention plus feed-forward, and each only adds a change to the token's vector; the vector itself is never replaced. (Real layers also normalise the vector before each step.)
captions.s47-layer-stack: Stack 64 of them and the vector is refined 64 times, picking up more abstract meaning as it goes. (The arrow's path is invented to show the idea.)

captions.s48-last-token: After the last layer, the vector at the final position has soaked up everything needed to predict the next token.
captions.s49-dot-vocab: Its dot product with every row of the output table, lm_head, gives 248,320 scores, called logits. Qwen3.8-27B keeps lm_head separate from its embedding table. (The five scores are toys.)

captions.s50-temperature: Temperature divides every score before the softmax. Below 1 the gaps stretch and the top word wins by more; above 1 they squeeze together and the choice flattens.
captions.s51-softmax-probs: Softmax turns the scores into probabilities: raise e to each one and divide by the total. Every share is between 0 and 1, and together they add up to exactly 1.
captions.s52-top-k: Top-k keeps the k most likely tokens, here 3, rescales them to add up to 1 again, and rolls a weighted die. That is why the same prompt can give different answers.

captions.s54-loop-closed: One forward pass: the embedder, 64 layers of attention and feed-forward, then sampling. The chosen token is appended and the whole stack runs again for the next one. (In practice the model caches work from earlier tokens; part 2 covers that.)

captions.x01-trainpass: Training runs this very same pass. The guess is scored against the real next word, and the error flows back to nudge every number in every stage. Inference is the same pass with the numbers frozen.

captions.t002-left-off: Part 1 in one row: tokens become vectors, 64 layers of attention and feed-forward turn them into scores across 248,320 vocabulary slots, and sampling picks the next token. That token is appended and the row runs again.

captions.t003-two-threads: Part 2 follows two threads: how the model behaves (fine-tuning, reasoning, alignment) and what it costs to serve (mixture of experts, the GPU, the KV cache, quantization). (Illustrative.)

captions.t101-base-continues: A base model only continues the document. Given the instruction to return "This is a test", the actual answer gets only 0.01 probability, while plausible continuations like forum replies take the rest. (Toy numbers.)

captions.t102-sft-pairs: Fine-tuning trains the model on pairs: the instruction, and the answer we want it to give. Nudging the weights toward the good answer teaches the model to answer instead of rambling. (Toy example.)

captions.t103-dolly-row: One real row from Databricks Dolly 15k: an instruction about Lollapalooza, context, and a human-written answer. Thousands of demonstrations like this turn a base model into an instruct model.

captions.t104-chat-template: The chat template wraps every message in role markers, opening with im_start and closing with im_end. It ends with the assistant cue, so the model starts writing its reply. (Real Qwen3.8-27B template render and token ids.)
captions.t105-control-tokens: Pre-training text like "I can dependably deploy LLMs" never uses control tokens like im_start and im_end. Fine-tuning teaches the model what they mean: where a turn opens, where it closes, and where to stop writing. (Real Qwen3.8-27B tokens.)

captions.t106-template-knobs: Template switches change the prompt before the model ever sees it, without touching any weights. Flipping switches can drop the assistant cue, turn off thinking, or inject a low reasoning-effort instruction. (Real Qwen3.8-27B template options.)

captions.t107-tool-calling: A model that follows instructions can be taught to emit a tool call when it needs a calculator. The runtime executes the call and returns the answer as text, repeating the loop into an agent. (Illustrative.)

captions.t201-imitation-cap: When a question like 17 x 24 has one right answer, imitation can only match the examples. When there are ten good answers to a crash question, there is nothing single to copy. (Toy illustration.)

captions.t202-try-and-grade: The model answers 17 x 24 four times, and a program checks only the final number: 408 earns a reward of 1, anything else 0. (Toy numbers; real training samples 8 to 64 attempts per question.)
captions.t203-advantage: Comparing each attempt with the 0.5 average gives the advantage: the two 408 answers get +0.5, while the wrong answers get -0.5. That relative signal is what decides which attempts to reinforce. (Toy numbers.)
captions.t204-reinforce: Nudging the weights toward positive advantages makes working step by step grow from 0.30 to 0.32 after one update. Repeat that over a million prompts, and working step by step reaches 0.92 to become the default. (Toy numbers.)

captions.t205-score-source: Some tasks can be checked by code: checking for 408 gives reward 1, and passing 7 of 10 unit tests gives 0.7. For subjective answers with no checkable outcome, a separate reward model scores the text. (Toy numbers.)
captions.t206-reward-model: Thousands of human A/B choices train the reward model to predict which answer people prefer. Once trained, it gives any answer a score like 0.82 and stands in for human raters inside the loop. (Toy numbers.)

captions.t207-imitate-vs-discover: Imitation can only reproduce what is inside the training data. Because reinforcement learning only checks the final outcome, the model can discover a winning approach that nobody wrote down. (Illustrative.)

captions.t208-think-tokens: Thinking tokens inside the think tags are ordinary tokens generated and appended to the context one at a time. Each thinking token costs one more trip round the Part 1 loop before the answer begins. (Real Qwen3.8-27B marker ids.)

captions.t209-cold-start: Seed data for a reasoning model already contains the reasoning: this OpenR1-Math-220k row thinks for 2,205 tokens before it answers. Fine-tuning on rows like it teaches the think-then-answer format, and reinforcement learning takes over from there. (Not Qwen's own data; the kind used for a cold start.)

captions.t301-obedience: An instruct model is trained to obey, not to judge. A request to draft an email goes through, and a request that should be refused passes through the same open gate. (Illustrative.)
captions.t302-repeat-anything: Asked to repeat that banks are pure evil, the instruct model echoes the sentence word for word. Training taught it to follow the instruction without weighing what it says. (Toy example.)

captions.t303-chosen-rejected: Safety tuning pairs the banks prompt with two answers: the repeated sentence as the rejected answer, and a measured reply as the chosen one. (Toy example.)
captions.t304-preference-nudge: One round on the pair raises the chosen answer from 0.10 to 0.45 and pushes the rejected repetition down from 0.60 to 0.12. Nudging the weights shifts what the model prefers without wiping out what it knows. (Toy numbers.)

captions.t305-safety-data: Real safety data has the same shape at scale: PKU-SafeRLHF has 82,118 rows across 16 columns, each with a prompt, two candidate responses and safety labels. Because the text includes harmful prompts, the dataset is inspected by schema and row counts rather than raw rows.

captions.t306-model-names: Model name suffixes tell you what was done to the weights. Suffixes like -it and -instruct mean the model follows instructions, while -heretic and -abliterated mean safety refusals were deliberately stripped out. (Illustrative.)

captions.t401-dense-touches-all: A dense model runs every weight for every single token: a 5,120-number vector expands through Wu to 17,408 numbers and back through Wd. One token costs about 24 billion multiply-adds across the whole model.
captions.t402-wasted: Most of the 17,408 numbers are weak, and the silencing step collapses them near zero so their matching rows in Wd are multiplied by zero. A dense model still computes every one of those multiply-adds anyway. (Toy activations.)

captions.t403-not-all-knowledge: A dense feed-forward block holds all the model knows, but the token le only needs French and def only needs Python syntax. Activating the whole block for every word does far more work than the token needs. (Illustrative.)
captions.t404-split-into-experts: Splitting the feed-forward block cuts it into smaller blocks called experts, each with its own Wu and Wd. A small router matrix sits in front of them to decide which experts a token should visit. (Toy architecture.)

captions.t405-router-scores: The router dots the token vector with each expert's column to get one score per expert: four products for E2 add up to 2.10. E2 and E5 get the highest scores, while the other six score lower. (Toy numbers.)
captions.t406-top2: Only the top two experts run: E2 and E5 produce outputs, while the other six sit out. Softmax turns their scores of 2.1 and 1.8 into weights of 0.57 and 0.43, scaling their outputs before adding them back onto the token. (Toy numbers.)

captions.t407-different-experts: Every token runs the router again to pick its own pair: le chooses E2 and E5, def chooses E1 and E7, and knight chooses E3 and E8. Each lit cell shows the softmax weight that expert receives for that token. (Toy numbers.)

captions.t408-router-learns: You cannot nudge an all-or-nothing choice a little at a time, so the top-two switch gives no smooth training signal. Training nudges the softmax weights instead: raising E2's score moves the weights from 0.57 and 0.43 to 0.62 and 0.38 when E2 helps. (Toy numbers.)
captions.t409-load-balance: Left alone, favored experts get picked more, improve faster, and soon handle almost every token while the rest are wasted. Training adds a balancing penalty that pushes each expert's share back toward one eighth. (Toy simulation.)

captions.t410-total-vs-active: Total parameters are what the model stores, while active parameters are what one token actually uses. Dense Qwen3.8-27B uses all 27.8B (100%), while sparse Mixtral uses 12.9B of 46.7B (28%) and DeepSeek-V3 uses 37B of 671B (6%).
captions.t411-memory-not-compute: Mixtral computes like a 12.9B model, but every one of its 46.7B parameters must stay loaded in GPU memory because any expert could be picked next. In BF16, holding those weights alone requires 93.4 GB of memory before adding the cache.

captions.t501-independent-dots: Multiplying a token vector by Wu is just one independent dot product per column: nothing branches and nothing waits. The real Wu has 17,408 columns, and a GPU calculates all of them at once. (Toy dimensions.)

captions.t502-cpu-vs-gpu: Given 160 cells of work, an eight-core CPU finishes eight cells per tick and needs 20 ticks. A GPU uses roughly 400 simpler lanes to finish every cell in a single tick. (Illustrative.)
captions.t503-cpu-overhead: A CPU spends most of its clock cycles on coordination: fetching numbers into registers, reading accumulators, and looping to the next pair. The actual multiplication is only a tiny sliver of each step. (Illustrative.)

captions.t504-tensor-core: A standard core does one multiply-add at a time, but a tensor core swallows whole matrix tiles at once. Multiplying two 16x16 tiles computes 4,096 multiply-adds from a single instruction. (Toy tiles.)
captions.t505-keep-the-sum: Matrix products are computed tile by tile, keeping the running sum in fast registers as it steps through the shared dimension. Storing the partial sums on-chip means the finished tile is written out to memory only once. (Toy tiles.)

captions.t506-kernel-schedules: A kernel chops large matrices into tiles and stages them down the memory ladder from VRAM into shared memory, registers, and tensor cores. Scheduling this flow keeps tensor cores fed so they never sit idle waiting for data. (Illustrative.)
captions.t507-cuda-to-silicon: Code written in CUDA C++ compiles into PTX, an assembly-like language that stays stable across GPU generations. The compiler then turns PTX into the specific machine code that the silicon actually executes.

captions.t601-gandalf-loop: The loop from Part 1 runs on the 18 tokens of the Gandalf sentence. The model predicts the next token " not", appends it to make 19 tokens, and takes another trip round the loop to produce " pass".
captions.t602-redo-everything: Taken literally, every step recomputes q, k and v for every token: two new tokens cost 18 + 19 = 37 recomputed old ones, in every one of the 64 layers. (Schematic of one layer.)

captions.t603-old-never-change: Because tokens only look backward, appending " not" to the Gandalf sentence adds a seventh row to the score table without altering the six rows above it. Everything computed for earlier tokens stays frozen forever. (Toy numbers.)

captions.t604-keep-kv-drop-q: The cache stores the key and value of each earlier token so they never need recomputing. The newest token computes its own query, compares it against the stored keys, and drops the query once the step finishes. (Toy vectors.)
captions.t605-decode-step: To predict " pass", only the new token " not" computes its vectors: its query dots against the six cached keys to weight the cached values into an output. Its key and value are then appended to the cache for future steps. (Toy numbers.)

captions.t606-kv-memory: Qwen3.8-27B keeps 64 KiB of keys and values per token in its 16 full-attention layers: 0.25 GiB at a 4k context and 16 GiB at the full 262k, for every request in flight. Four requests at 131k add about 32 GiB of cache to the 51.7 GiB of weights.

captions.t607-prefill-vs-decode: Prefill reads the 51.7 GiB of weights once and applies them across all prompt tokens together, keeping the GPU compute-bound. Decode generates only one new token per step, having to stream those same weights from memory for every single token.
captions.t608-two-phases: Inference has two bottlenecks with different feels: time-to-first-token is the compute-bound prefill batch, while inter-token delay is the memory-bandwidth-bound decode stream. SREs must tune each phase with different tools. (Illustrative.)

captions.t609-decode-limit: A single-stream decode step reads all 55.6 GB of BF16 weights to produce one token, so speed is capped by memory bandwidth divided by model size. Bandwidths of 1,000, 2,000, and 3,000 GB/s yield rough speed ceilings of 18, 36, and 54 tokens per second. (Illustrative.)

captions.t701-bits: One unsigned 8-bit number, 180: flip its leftmost bit and it drops to 52, flip the rightmost and it only moves to 181. Not every bit matters equally. (A toy integer, not a real weight format.)

captions.t702-memory-formula: Memory footprint is parameters times bytes per weight: Qwen3.8-27B needs 111.1 GB in FP32, 55.6 GB in BF16, 27.8 GB in 8-bit, and 13.9 GB in 4-bit. A real FP8 repository weighs 30.9 GB because it also includes the per-block scale tensors.

captions.t703-fewer-bits: 32 real weights from Qwen3.8-27B, the first 32 of layer 3's Wu, before and after rounding to int4: each moves to the nearest of 16 levels, and storage drops from 2 bytes to about half a byte per weight. Over the first 327,680 weights of that matrix the error is about a tenth of the weights' spread (0.097).
captions.t704-snap-to-levels: The 32 real weights sit on a number line, snapping to the 16 available INT4 levels defined by the group scale of 0.0039. The grey error ticks show how far each weight moved, producing a relative error of 0.097 over the first 327,680 weights of that matrix.

captions.t705-float-anatomy: A floating-point number splits bits into sign, exponent (dynamic range), and mantissa (precision). BF16 retains FP32's 8 exponent bits while trimming the mantissa to 7, preserving the same range in half the bytes.

captions.t706-block-scales: Sixteen levels are too coarse for a full tensor, so 4-bit formats store a separate scale for each small block of weights. NVFP4 uses blocks of 16 values with an FP8 scale, while GGUF formats mix precisions to average about 4.9 bits for Q4_K_M and about 4.7 for Q4_K_S. (Toy values.)

captions.t707-gptq-awq: Rounding each weight on its own lets small errors pile up in the output. GPTQ picks the roundings so the errors cancel, and AWQ scales up the few weights that meet the biggest inputs so they survive rounding. (Toy numbers.)

captions.t708-kernel-speaks-format: A 4-bit format packs two values into each byte alongside a scale factor. Kernels like Marlin and Machete unpack those bytes, attach the scale, and feed the values into tensor cores so the format can run fast. (Toy bytes.)
captions.t709-native-support: Quantization only speeds up inference if the GPU can multiply that format directly in silicon. Whether a chip natively executes FP8 or FP4 depends on its generation, leading directly to the hardware choices in Part 3. (Illustrative.)

captions.d001-g7e-size-ladder: The g7e family scales from one to eight 96 GB GDDR7 GPUs, and the article picks g7e.2xlarge for one GPU per node. (Real g7e specs, from the AWS docs at the time of this deployment.)

captions.d002-regions-quota: g7e is offered in 13 of the 39 AWS Regions, and the on-demand G and VT quota is measured in vCPU: 80 vCPU allows 10 g7e.2xlarges. (Real AWS docs at the time of this deployment; quota example is arithmetic.)

captions.d102-bottlerocket-anatomy: A Bottlerocket node stacks a read-only verified root, tmpfs /etc, writable /local and SELinux over an admin API, with the NVIDIA stack baked in. (Illustrative.)

captions.d201-memory-budget: At 0.90 utilization a 94.97 GiB card gives vLLM 85.47 GiB, and after 22.13 GiB of weights and 4.08 GiB of other memory, 59.26 GiB is left as the KV cache pool. (Measured on a running pod, vLLM v0.28.0.)

captions.d202-kv-block: The 17 layer groups share one 53.125 MiB block size: an attention block holds 1,600 tokens of K and V, a state block holds one state copy. An 8,192 token request therefore needs 6 + 15 = 21 blocks. (Computed for fp8 KV and MTP 3; the block size and pool match a running pod's log.)

captions.d203-prefix-grid: Prefix cache hits land on whole 1,600 token blocks, and with MTP on vLLM recomputes the last matched block, so a 1,700 token shared prefix gets 0 hit tokens and a 3,400 token one gets 1,600. (Block size as logged by a running pod; the recompute rule is from the vLLM v0.32.0 source.)

captions.d204-streamer-pipeline: The Run:ai Model Streamer reads shards from S3 with concurrent clients into a CPU buffer while earlier tensors are already being copied to the GPU, where the default loader copies everything first. (Illustrative timing, not a benchmark.)

captions.d301-round-robin-vs-epp: Round robin sends the next request to pod C whatever its state; the picker filters, scores every pod with the built-in weights 2/2/3, and sends the request straight to pod B. (Toy numbers.)

captions.d302-three-signals: The picker scrapes load from vLLM every 50 ms, but prefix hits come from its own record of what it routed where; precise KV events are opt-in, so the default in llm-d v1.0.0 is A plus B. (Illustrative.)

captions.d303-weights-exchange-rate: With weights 2/2/3 the prefix-warm pod keeps winning until the 0.8 filter drops it; with 2/3/1 an idle pod takes over at KV 0.43, and one queued request moves the stock break-even to 0.60. (Simulated.)

captions.d401-control-and-data-plane: Envoy Gateway already watches the Gateway API kinds and programs the proxy pod; the AI Gateway adds a second controller, extension hooks on gRPC port 1063, and an ai-gateway-extproc container (2/2 becomes 3/3). The install order shown ran clean on kind, the docs order did not. (Validated on kind.)

captions.d402-request-path: The model comes from the request body: the ai-gateway-extproc sidecar sets x-ai-eg-model (overwriting any client value), Envoy matches the route on it, and the endpoint picker chooses the pod. Token usage on the way back becomes four gen_ai histograms. (Validated on kind with test doubles.)

captions.d501-run-simulation: With the built-in default weights (queue 2, KV 2, prefix 3) the shared system prompt keeps landing on pod A, until its queue reaches 5 and the filter sends request 8 to pod B. (Simulated: fake pods, not a GPU.)

captions.d502-metric-birthplaces: Every metric is born at one stage of a request, and the picker turns the pod gauges into the pool averages that KEDA reads. (Illustrative: stage widths are not to scale.)

captions.d503-hit-ratio: Four vLLM prefix cache counters with toy values: 1,200,000 queried, 840,000 local hits, 360,000 connector queries, 90,000 connector hits give a 77.5% cached share and 270,000 computed tokens, but pods at 70% and 50% on 1:2 traffic give 56.7% when you sum first then divide, not 60%. And a histogram quantile is an interpolation inside a bucket, so the bucket edges set the resolution. (Toy numbers.)

captions.d601-keda-ownership: KEDA owns the 0 to 1 replica step on a 30s poll and the HPA owns 1 to N on a 15s sync, choosing the max over triggers. A burst climbs the pod to 8 after a 120s scale-up window, and a 1800s window slows the scale down to one pod at a time. (Illustrative.)

captions.d603-value-vs-averagevalue: 4 replicas, EPP average queue 3, threshold 2: AverageValue computes ceil(3/2) = 2 and scales down, while Value computes ceil(4 x 3/2) = 6 and scales up. The default metricType is AverageValue, which drops the current-replica term, so per-pod triggers need metricType: Value. (Toy numbers.)

captions.d602-scale-out-chain: From a rising metric to served traffic: the HPA adds a replica on a 15s sync loop (30s at 0 to 1 on the KEDA poll), then the pod is Pending, Karpenter launches a node, the image is pulled and the weights load, and readiness passes. The drawing gives every hop the same width on purpose: on my pod, startup took 407 seconds from the first log line to the API server, while the node launch and the image pull come before that line. Early-warning triggers start the chain before users feel the load. (Illustrative.)

captions.d701-tier-ladder: Each prompt chunk is written through to CPU RAM and NVMe as it completes, so eviction drops only one copy and a hit loads from the nearest tier that has it, and the NVMe tier needs a cleanup sidecar because vLLM never deletes its files. The CPU and NVMe token counts use 34 KiB per token at fp8, the GPU pool is the measured 59.26 GiB counted in blocks because it also holds state, and the CPU and NVMe sizes are examples. (Measured GPU pool, example tier sizes.)

captions.d702-prefix-hit-tiers: The same shared prefix is loaded up from the nearest tier that still holds it, staged through CPU RAM when it sits on NVMe, and recomputed in full when no tier has it. The 12,800-token prefix is a toy length, the 1,600-token chunk is the block size a running pod logs, and no timings are shown because AWS publishes only IOPS for the g7e local NVMe, not MB/s. (Illustrative.)
